Preschool Programs - City of Piedmont Last item for navigation City of Piedmont » Departments » Recreation » Preschool ProgramsShare ThisPrint Page A+Increase Font A-decrease font The Piedmont Recreation Department offers four play-based preschool programs for children ages 2–5 years. Our team of preschool educators is committed to providing a warm and safe environment to best support children's natural curiosity and enthusiasm for learning. We are dedicated to the development of a school/home community in which teachers and families learn and grow together. Come explore PRD's play-based preschool programs and experience what it's like to be a part of OUR community! To view PRD's current Preschool Parent Handbook, please click HERE Preschool Program Locations Piedmont Community Hall, Lower Level, 711 Highland Avenue Tiddlywinks (2 Years) Pre-K (4 & 5 Years) 801 Magnolia East Wing, 801 Magnolia Avenue* Hillside Playschool (3 & 4 Years) Wildwood Schoolmates Building, 301 Wildwood Avenue* Skipping Stones (3 & 4 Years) *Due to the construction schedule of the Piedmont Community Pool, these programs have been relocated. Preschool 2024/2025 School Year Dates Monday–Thursday, August 19, 2024–May 22, 2025 Days/Hours vary by program 2023/2024 School Year Note: Preschool enrollment is at capacity. messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What are the different shapes of galaxies and what are some examples of each shape?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Galaxies come in a variety of shapes, mostly spirals and ellipticals, as well as those with less orderly appearances, usually dubbed irregular.  Spiral galaxies have a pancake-like disk of stars and a central bulge or tight concentration of stars. The spiral arms can be wound tightly or loosely, and some cannot be seen from Earth because we view the galaxy from the side, edge on. The Milky Way, our home galaxy, and the Andromeda galaxies are examples of spiral galaxies. There is also a subtype known as barred spirals, which sport ribbons of stars, gas, and dust that cut across their centers.  Elliptical galaxies have shapes that range from completely round to oval and usually contain little gas and dust. The stars orbit around the core in random directions and are generally older than those in spiral galaxies since little of the gas needed to form new stars remains. An example of an elliptical galaxy is NGC 2865, located 100 million light-years away.  Irregular galaxies have unusual shapes, like toothpicks, rings, or even little groupings of stars. They range from dwarf irregular galaxies with 100 million times the Sun’s mass to large ones weighing 10 billion solar masses. Some irregular galaxies may be new, formed by material pulled from encounters with other galaxies.

They are less common than spiral galaxies.Unlike spirals, elliptical galaxies usually contain little gas and dust and show very little organization or structure. The stars orbit around the core in random directions and are generally older than those in spiral galaxies since little of the gas needed to form new stars remains. Scientists think elliptical galaxies originate from collisions and mergers with spirals.Lenticular GalaxiesLenticular galaxy NGC 4886, imaged here by the Hubble Space Telescope, contains primarily old stars but no spiral arms.ESA/Hubble & NASA. Acknowledgement: Gilles ChapdelaineLenticular galaxies are a kind of cross between spirals and ellipticals. They have the central bulge and disk common to spiral galaxies but no arms. But like ellipticals, lenticular galaxies have older stellar populations and little ongoing star formation.Scientists have a few theories about how lenticular galaxies evolved. One idea suggests these galaxies are older spirals whose arms have faded. Another proposes that lenticulars formed from mergers of spiral galaxies.Irregular GalaxiesThe Hubble Space Telescope captured this image of NGC 5264, an irregular dwarf galaxy.ESA/Hubble & NASAIrregular galaxies have unusual shapes, like toothpicks, rings, or even little groupings of stars. They range from dwarf irregular galaxies with 100 million times the Sun’s mass to large ones weighing 10 billion solar masses.Astronomers think these galaxies’ odd shapes are sometimes the result of interactions with others. For example, one spiral galaxy passing another with a stronger gravitational pull could lose some of its material, become distorted, and morph into a new shape. Some, like gas-rich dwarf galaxies, may be new, formed by material pulled from such encounters. Or perhaps when galaxies collide, they create a larger, oddly shaped mashup.

messages.text: Why do scientists think that the presence of a bar in spiral galaxies indicates that they have reached full maturity?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Scientists think that the presence of a bar in spiral galaxies indicates that they have reached full maturity because the bar is a result of the galaxy's disk of stars and interstellar medium becoming more dominant over its bulge component. The formation of a bar is a sign of dynamical maturity in a spiral galaxy, as it represents a stage where the galaxy has developed a strong, organized structure. It is also associated with the presence of a central concentration of older stars, which further supports the idea of a galaxy reaching full maturity.

messages.text: What are active galaxies and how do they differ from inactive galaxies?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Active galaxies are a type of galaxy that have active galactic nuclei (AGN), characterized by their centers appearing more than 100 times brighter than the combined light of their stars, whereas inactive galaxies do not exhibit this excess brightness. The brightness in active galaxies is attributed to the accretion of matter by a supermassive black hole at their centers, forming an accretion disk that emits large amounts of energy across multiple wavelengths.  Active galaxies can be spiral, elliptical, or irregular, while inactive galaxies typically have less prominent or completely quiescent nuclei. The Milky Way, for example, is not currently an active galaxy, although it likely experienced a burst of activity in the past few million years.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What role do supermassive black holes play in active galaxies and how are they related to the brightness of these galaxies?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Supermassive black holes play a crucial role in active galaxies by powering their excess brightness. These black holes, with masses ranging from hundreds of thousands to billions of times the mass of our Sun, are located at the centers of active galaxies. Gas and dust collect around the black hole to form an accretion disk, which is then compressed and heated by the black hole's gravity, causing the material to glow across multiple wavelengths, from infrared to X-rays.  The brightness of active galaxies is directly related to the activity of their supermassive black holes. The more matter accreted by the black hole, the brighter the galaxy becomes. Infrared observations have revealed that black holes and their accretion disks are embedded within a clumpy ring of cooler dust, called a torus, which may be a few light-years across. Close to the black hole, a small fraction of the infalling gas can be driven outward, perpendicular to the disk, as jets of particles that move near the speed of light, further contributing to the galaxy's brightness.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How do astronomers classify active galaxies?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Astronomers classify active galaxies based on the distinctive characteristics and behaviors they observe as well as their brightness in radio wavelengths. During the early 20th century, scientists began classifying active galaxies by their appearance and behaviors, such as Seyfert galaxies, quasars, and BL Lacertae objects. However, scientists now think that viewing the centers of these galaxies at different angles can produce many of the signature traits, such as seeing directly into the torus versus seeing it from the side.  Active galaxies can also be categorized by their brightness in radio wavelengths, which can reveal information about their jet structures and the rate at which matter is being ejected from the galaxy's center. Astronomers use these classifications to better understand the physical processes occurring in active galaxies and the role supermassive black holes play in shaping their environments.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What is the relationship between the Ventura County Air Pollution Control District and the California Air Resources Board?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The Ventura County Air Pollution Control District is one of the local air districts governed by the California Air Resources Board. The California Air Resources Board is the state agency responsible for regulating air pollution in California. It sets guidelines and standards for air quality, and local air districts like the Ventura County APCD implement these standards at the local level. The Ventura County APCD is responsible for monitoring and enforcing air quality regulations within Ventura County.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What other areas does the California Air Resources Board oversee apart from Ventura County?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The California Air Resources Board oversees all 35 local air districts in California, not just Ventura County. These districts are responsible for regional air quality planning, monitoring, and stationary source and facility permitting within their respective jurisdictions. The districts also administer air quality improvement grant programs and work with the California Air Resources Board to ensure that all Californians breathe clean air.

messages.text: Is the Parks and Community Services Department in Dublin, CA responsible for the operation of The Wave at Emerald Glen Park?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Yes, the Parks and Community Services Department in Dublin, CA is responsible for the operation of The Wave at Emerald Glen Park. This includes year-round swim lessons, fitness swimming, the swim league champions, the Green Gators Swim Team, and a seasonal waterpark equipped with six waterslides and an aqua play feature for young kids.

The Sports division is responsible for Youth and  Adult Sports Leagues, Sports Fields and Courts, and the extremely popular Jr. Warriors Basketball Program. The Wave, located at Emerald Glen Park, offers year-round swim lessons, and fitness swimming, and is home to the swim league champions, the Green Gators Swim Team.  The Wave also includes a seasonal waterpark equipped with six waterslides and an aqua play feature for young kids.   The Heritage and Cultural Arts Division is responsible for Dublin Heritage Park & Museums and the Dublin Camp Parks Military History Center and the very robust permanent and temporary public art program. messages.text: How can I navigate the Minneapolis VA Medical Center using the interactive campus map and what are the driving directions from different locations?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: To navigate the Minneapolis VA Medical Center using the interactive campus map, you can visit the official VA Minneapolis Health Care website and look for the "Interactive campus map" section. Once there, you can select the department or building you need, and a moving route marker will lead you turn-by-turn to your destination.  For driving directions from the east (St. Paul), take Interstate 35E south to the West 7th Street/ State Route 5 exit. Continue on Route 5 to the Fort Snelling exit and stay to the right as you follow the exit around. You will "Y" into traffic coming from Mendota Bridge. Move to the right and exit on U.S. Route 55 west. As you exit, it will "Y" almost immediately. Stay to the left and go straight through the traffic light. You will be on Minnehaha Avenue. Follow Minnehaha Avenue to the traffic light in front of the medical center and turn left into the parking lot. Visitor and outpatient parking are located on your left.  If you're coming from the southeast, take Interstate 35E to State Route 110 west. Take the U.S. Route 55 west/Fort Snelling exit. At the top of the exit ramp, turn left to continue on U.S. 55 west. Go to the traffic light (Minnehaha Avenue) and turn left. Follow Minnehaha Avenue to the traffic light in front of the medical center and turn left into the lot. Visitor and outpatient parking are located on your left.  For directions from the west, take Interstate 494 east to Interstate 35W north. Take State Route 62 east. Get into the right lane on State Route 62 and exit on U.S. 55 west. At the top of the exit ramp, turn left to continue on U.S. 55 west. Go to the traffic light (Minnehaha Avenue) and turn left. Follow Minnehaha Avenue to the traffic light in front of the medical center and turn left into the lot. Visitor and outpatient parking are located on your left.

messages.text: What is Beneficiary Travel?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Beneficiary Travel is a program that provides transportation benefits to eligible patients, including round-trip transportation from your home to the medical center, mileage reimbursement, or special mode transport. Eligibility for the program may depend on various factors, such as the distance between your home and the medical center, the type of appointment, and your specific medical condition. To find out if you qualify for beneficiary travel benefits, I recommend contacting the Minneapolis VA Medical Center directly.

messages.text: What is the difference between the County of Albany and the County of Broome in New York State?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Albany County and Broome County are two different counties in New York State with their own unique characteristics.  Albany County is located in the Capital-Saratoga region and is home to the State Capital. It has a population of over 300,000. The County was established in 1683, making it one of the oldest counties in the state.  On the other hand, Broome County is located in the Central New York region and was named in honor of John Broome, who was lieutenant governor in 1806 when the County was established. Broome County is known for its agriculture and farming, and it is home to Binghamton University.  In terms of size, Albany County is larger with an area of 530 square miles, while Broome County spans 715 square miles.  Both counties have their own elected officials and municipalities, with Broome County being governed by a County Executive and a Chairperson of the Legislature, and Albany County being governed by a County Executive and a 39-member Legislature.

Binghamton University is a public research university with a strong reputation for its programs in engineering, business, and the liberal arts. It is also home to several research centers and institutes, including the Center for Advanced Microelectronics Manufacturing and the Institute for Material Research.  Broome Community College is a two-year college that offers associate's degrees and certificates in a variety of fields, including business, health sciences, and technology. The college also has transfer agreements with several four-year institutions, allowing students to easily transfer to a bachelor's degree program.  Davis College is a private Christian college that offers associate's and bachelor's degrees in fields such as business, criminal justice, and religious studies. The college has a strong focus on spiritual development and service, and offers a variety of opportunities for students to get involved in community service and missions.  Ridley-Lowell Business and Technical Institute is a private career school that offers programs in fields such as business, healthcare, and information technology. The school has a strong focus on preparing students for entry-level positions in their chosen field, and offers a variety of hands-on learning opportunities.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How does the vacation system work for Broome County employees?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Broome County offers a competitive vacation plan to all regular full-time employees and regular IBM employees who work alternative work schedules. All regular full-time IBM employees receive a minimum of 15 days paid vacation each year. Vacation time is based on years of service and type of employment. Full-time employees are entitled to 15, 20, or 25 days of vacation per year, depending on their years of service. Supplemental employees are entitled to 10, 15, or 20 days of vacation per year, depending on their years of service. Vacation can be taken at any time of the year, but the full amount isn't earned until year-end. Employees can take vacation time in weeks, days, or half days, and they may take their accrued vacation before they have earned it. However, vacation taken before it's earned is considered a salary advance. If an employee separates from IBM before they earn the vacation they have taken, IBM will seek reimbursement for the value of the unearned days. Vacation pay is at the same rate as an employee's regular salary or hourly pay, and all vacation pay is subject to tax withholding. Employees don't have the option of choosing cash payments over taking vacation time from work. In the year of hire, rehire, or conversion from supplemental to regular employment, vacation is based on the number of days worked during the year. Employees on flexible work week schedules earn vacation based on hours worked per week and years of service.

messages.text: How does the HEASARC archive differ from the LAMBDA archive?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The HEASARC was originally the primary archive for NASA's missions studying electromagnetic radiation from extremely energetic cosmic phenomena ranging from black holes to the Big Bang. After merging with the Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis (LAMBDA) in 2008, the HEASARC archive expanded to include data obtained by high-energy astronomy missions observing in the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV), X-ray, and gamma-ray bands, as well as data from space missions, balloons, and ground-based facilities that have studied the relic cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation in the sub-mm, mm and cm bands.  On the other hand, LAMBDA is a "multi-mission NASA center of expertise for cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation research; it provides CMB researchers with archive data from cosmology missions, software tools, and links to other sites of interest". Since the merger, LAMBDA's expertise and data are incorporated within the HEASARC.  However, the specific differences between the archives in terms of data organization, access, and utilization might not be entirely clear without directly accessing the databases or referring to documentation specific to each archive.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What is the difference between the Swift XRT CALDB and NuSTAR FPM caldb?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The Swift XRT CALDB (Calibration Database) and NuSTAR FPM caldb (Focus Position Mask) are both calibration databases for specific astronomical instruments, but they serve different observatories and have unique characteristics.  The Swift XRT CALDB is associated with the X-ray Telescope (XRT) on the Swift observatory. It provides calibration files necessary for processing and analyzing XRT data, including information about the instrument's sensitivity, noise, and background.  The NuSTAR FPM caldb, on the other hand, is related to the Focus Position Mask of the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) observatory. It offers calibration files for the NuSTAR's focal plane modules (FPMs) that enable precise localization of X-ray sources and corrections for distortions and other effects.  In short, the Swift XRT CALDB and NuSTAR FPM caldb serve different observatories, instruments, and purposes in calibrating and analyzing data.

messages.text: What is the relationship between the HEASARC and the Virtual Observatory?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive Research Center (HEASARC) is part of the Virtual Observatory (VO), which is an international initiative to provide a single, unified interface for accessing and analyzing astronomical data from various sources and archives. As a VO member, HEASARC ensures comprehensive and consistent VO access to NASA mission datasets. Users can now query the HEASARC's catalogs using VO-enabled services and specialized tools. Additionally, HEASARC is involved in other VO activities and collaborates with other VO members and NASA archives.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How does the HEASARC archive serve the education and public outreach community?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The HEASARC archive serves the education and public outreach community in several ways:  1. Educational resources: HEASARC offers educational resources such as Imagine the Universe!, StarChild (K-8 EPO), and WebStars, which provide general astronomy information, news, and learning materials for students, teachers, and the public.  2. Publicly accessible data: The HEASARC archive contains data from numerous NASA and other space agency missions, which are publicly accessible and can be used for educational and outreach purposes.  3. Visual content: HEASARC provides images, spectra, light curves, and other visual content that can be used to support educational and public outreach initiatives.  4. Tools and services: HEASARC offers various tools and services, such as the Picture of the Week, Astronomy Picture of the Day, and other image collections, which can be used for educational and public outreach purposes.  5. Collaboration: HEASARC collaborates with other organizations and initiatives to support educational and public outreach efforts, such as by providing data, tools, and expertise to educational programs, workshops, and conferences.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How does the HEASARC archive support researchers and scientists?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The HEASARC archive supports researchers and scientists in various ways:  1. Comprehensive data archive: HEASARC serves as the primary archive for NASA's missions studying electromagnetic radiation from extremely energetic cosmic phenomena, providing researchers with a wealth of data for analysis and research.  2. Data access and retrieval: HEASARC offers tools and services for accessing, retrieving, and manipulating archived data. These tools include the HEASARC Browse, which allows researchers to search for data by mission, target name, or observing date, and  the High Energy Astrophysics Data System (HEASARC) Archive Access, which enables researchers to download data directly from the archive.  3. Data analysis software: HEASARC provides a variety of data analysis software tools, such as FTOOLS, XRONOS, and XIMAGE, which can be used to analyze and process archived data from various missions and experiments.  4. Collaboration and support: HEASARC collaborates with researchers and scientists to provide expertise, guidance, and support in using archived data and analysis tools.  5. Virtual Observatory (VO) integration: HEASARC is a member of the NASA Astronomical Virtual Observatories (NAVO) and offers VO-enabled services, which enable researchers to access and interact with the HEASARC archive through specialized tools and services within the VO framework.

contexts.text: HEASARC Help Desk, Feedback, and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) HEASARC Help Desk, Feedback, and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) The HEASARC is a source of gamma-ray, X-ray, and extreme ultraviolet observations of cosmic (non-solar) sources. This site provides access to archival data , associated analysis software, web tools, and mission-specific and general documentation, as well as relevant educational and outreach material. In addition, this site provides a number of general astronomical tools such as time, energy and coordinate converters, SkyView, which allows users to obtain multiwaveband images of the sky, and the Xamin and Browse interfaces, which allow users to identify and/or select resources from the HEASARC and also a number of other external archives, e.g., VizieR. To access archival data from other energy ranges, you can also visit the NASA Infra-red (IRSA), Microwave Background (LAMBDA, see below) , and UV/optical (MAST) archives, as well as the astrophysics service of the NSSDC. The LAMBDA (Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis) component of HEASARC is a "multi-mission NASA center of expertise for cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation research; it provides CMB researchers with archive data from cosmology missions, software tools, and links to other sites of interest". Feedback If you have suggestions, praise or complaints about our services, or if you have a question which is not one of those addressed in the list below, please send an email to the HEASARC via our Feedback form: be sure to select the most appropriate mailing list from the pull-down menu on the Feedback form to ensure the fastest response. HEASARC: NASA's Archive of Data on Energetic Phenomena The High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive Research Center (HEASARC) is the primary archive for NASA's (and other space agencies') missions studying electromagnetic radiation from extremely energetic cosmic phenomena ranging from black holes to the Big Bang. Since its merger with the Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis (LAMBDA) in 2008, the HEASARC archive contains data obtained by high-energy astronomy missions observing in the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV), X-ray, and gamma-ray bands, as well as data from space missions, balloons, and ground-based facilities that have studied the relic cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation in the sub-mm, mm and cm bands. The HEASARC is a member of the NASA Astronomical Virtual Observatories (NAVO) where we work with other NASA archives to ensure comprehensive and consistent VO access to NASA mission datasets. Users may now query the HEASARC's catalogs using VO-enabled services and specialized tools. This page describes how to get to the HEASARC VO-enabled services and provides information on other HEASARC VO activities. messages.text: What is the difference between the mileage reimbursement rate for VA health facilities and non-VA health facilities?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: There is no difference in the mileage reimbursement rate for VA health facilities and non-VA health facilities. The current rate is 41.5 cents ($0.415) per mile for approved, health-related travel. This rate is calculated based on the fastest and shortest route from your home to the closest VA or authorized non-VA health facility that can provide the care you need.

contexts.text: Reimbursed VA Travel Expenses And Mileage Rate | Veterans Affairs In some cases, we may reimburse you for the actual cost, up to 50% of the local government employee rate, for meals or lodging. You’ll need to provide all receipts. We determine the need for meals and lodging based on these factors: Your medical condition, and How far you need to travel for care, and Other circumstances Except in certain unusual cases, you can only get this reimbursement if we approve it before you travel. We won’t reimburse you for lodging or meals if you chose to stop or take a less direct route to a VA or VA-authorized health facility. Transportation to a non-VA health facility in an emergency  We can provide travel in certain emergency situations. If you have an emergency while receiving care at a VA health facility and the facility can’t provide the care you need: We may pay for your transport to a non-VA facility for emergency treatment and back to the VA facility. As long as we’ve approved the care at the non-VA facility, we’ll pay for this transportation—even if you’re not eligible for VA travel pay. If you have an emergency and you’re anywhere other than at a VA health facility: We may pay for your transport to a non-VA facility for emergency treatment. Contact your local facility within 72 hours of the emergency transport to determine your specific eligibility. This includes appointments scheduled on a day when you’re working at the same VA health facility. For unscheduled appointments, we may reimburse you for one-way travel if you’re seen as a Veteran and not an employee. messages.text: What is the California Air Resources Board and what are its key responsibilities?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The California Air Resources Board (CARB) is a state agency responsible for protecting public health from the harmful effects of air pollution. Its key responsibilities include guiding the activities of 35 local air pollution control districts, addressing global climate change, leading the state's efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions, setting the state's air quality standards, identifying health risk pollutants, measuring progress in reducing pollutants, verifying automakers' emissions compliance, researching air pollution problems and potential solutions, and studying the costs and benefits of pollution controls. CARB also holds monthly public meetings to review progress and consider new approaches to cleaning California's air.

contexts.text: About | California Air Resources Board The Governor can choose any of the board members to serve as the Chair.The other four include two who represent environmental justice communities (one appointed by the Senate and the other by the Assembly) and two nonvoting members appointed for Legislative oversight, one each from the Senate and Assembly.In July 2018, the Board established staggered six-year terms for voting members pursuant to AB 197.More InformationBoard StaffThe work of the Board is supported by a diverse professional staff of scientists, engineers, economists, lawyers and policy makers who collectively make up one of the world’s most respected environmental organizations.Partners for Clean AirThe Board is part of a coordinated three-tiered approach to cleaning up air pollution:The United States Environmental Protection Agency sets nationwide air quality and emissions standards and oversees state efforts and enforcement.The California Air Resources Board focuses on California’s unique air quality challenges by setting the state’s own stricter emissions standards for a range of statewide pollution sources including vehicles, fuels and consumer products.Thirty-five local air pollution control districts regulate emissions from businesses and stationary facilities, ranging from oil refineries to auto body shops and dry cleaners.Responsibilities & Work of CARBReducing air pollution and protecting public health guide CARB’s actions. Our role is to:Lead California’s efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions through measures that promote a more energy-efficient and resilient economy;Set the state’s air quality standards at levels that protect those at greatest risk – children, older adults and people with lung and heart disease;Identify pollutants that pose the greatest health risks, such as diesel exhaust particles, benzene in gasoline and formaldehyde in consumer products;Measure our progress in reducing pollutants utilizing the nation’s most extensive air monitoring network;Verify automakers’ emissions compliance at CARB’s renowned Mary D. Nichols Laboratory in Riverside;Research the causes and effects of air pollution problems – and potential solutions – using the best available science and technology; andStudy the costs and benefits of pollution controls, paying particular attention to individuals and communities most at risk.Engaging the PublicCARB holds monthly public meetings to review progress and consider new approaches to cleaning California’s air.

About | California Air Resources Board Our role is to:Lead California’s efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions through measures that promote a more energy-efficient and resilient economy;Set the state’s air quality standards at levels that protect those at greatest risk – children, older adults and people with lung and heart disease;Identify pollutants that pose the greatest health risks, such as diesel exhaust particles, benzene in gasoline and formaldehyde in consumer products;Measure our progress in reducing pollutants utilizing the nation’s most extensive air monitoring network;Verify automakers’ emissions compliance at CARB’s renowned Mary D. Nichols Laboratory in Riverside;Research the causes and effects of air pollution problems – and potential solutions – using the best available science and technology; andStudy the costs and benefits of pollution controls, paying particular attention to individuals and communities most at risk.Engaging the PublicCARB holds monthly public meetings to review progress and consider new approaches to cleaning California’s air. The Board, Chair and staff routinely consult industry and scientific experts and actively engage with advocates for public health, regulated businesses and low-income communities as part of the decision-making process.Helping the Most Impacted CommunitiesHeavily urbanized communities and those adjacent to busy freight corridors are particularly burdened with air pollution. This is especially true of neighborhoods sandwiched between freeways, ports and rail yards. CARB has a range of programs in place, with others ready under a new law (AB 617) to address pollution in these areas.AccomplishmentsCARB establishes state air quality regulations which protect public health by addressing all major sources of smog-forming air pollution, and other forms of air pollution. As a result, cars today are 99 percent cleaner than in the 1970s, resulting in less air pollution overall, shorter hospital stays and fewer days missed from school and work due to respiratory and cardiopulmonary diseases.California regulations, based on extensive research and sound science, have driven innovation, leading to significant technological developments such as the catalytic converter (which helped slash ozone by 60 percent), and the production of highly marketable low- and zero-emission cars and trucks, and cleaner fuels.The Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006 (Nunez) expanded CARB’s role to development and oversight of California’s main greenhouse gas reduction programs. These include cap-and-trade, the Low Carbon Fuel Standard and the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) programs.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How does the California Air Resources Board work with other organizations to clean up air pollution?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The California Air Resources Board is part of a coordinated three-tiered approach to cleaning up air pollution. The United States Environmental Protection Agency sets nationwide air quality and emissions standards and oversees state efforts and enforcement. The California Air Resources Board focuses on California's unique air quality challenges by setting the state's own stricter emissions standards for a range of statewide pollution sources including vehicles, fuels and consumer products. Thirty-five local air pollution control districts regulate emissions from businesses and stationary facilities, ranging from oil refineries to auto body shops and dry cleaners.

messages.text: What role does the California Air Resources Board play in reducing climate-changing emissions?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The California Air Resources Board leads California's efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions through measures that promote a more energy-efficient and resilient economy. The Board also verifies automakers’ emissions compliance at CARB’s renowned Mary D. Nichols Laboratory in Riverside.

messages.text: Does the California Air Resources Board conduct research on air pollution problems and potential solutions?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Yes, the California Air Resources Board conducts research on the causes and effects of air pollution problems – and potential solutions – using the best available science and technology. It also studies the costs and benefits of pollution controls, paying particular attention to individuals and communities most at risk.

About | California Air Resources Board Our role is to:Lead California’s efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions through measures that promote a more energy-efficient and resilient economy;Set the state’s air quality standards at levels that protect those at greatest risk – children, older adults and people with lung and heart disease;Identify pollutants that pose the greatest health risks, such as diesel exhaust particles, benzene in gasoline and formaldehyde in consumer products;Measure our progress in reducing pollutants utilizing the nation’s most extensive air monitoring network;Verify automakers’ emissions compliance at CARB’s renowned Mary D. Nichols Laboratory in Riverside;Research the causes and effects of air pollution problems – and potential solutions – using the best available science and technology; andStudy the costs and benefits of pollution controls, paying particular attention to individuals and communities most at risk.Engaging the PublicCARB holds monthly public meetings to review progress and consider new approaches to cleaning California’s air. The Board, Chair and staff routinely consult industry and scientific experts and actively engage with advocates for public health, regulated businesses and low-income communities as part of the decision-making process.Helping the Most Impacted CommunitiesHeavily urbanized communities and those adjacent to busy freight corridors are particularly burdened with air pollution. This is especially true of neighborhoods sandwiched between freeways, ports and rail yards. CARB has a range of programs in place, with others ready under a new law (AB 617) to address pollution in these areas.AccomplishmentsCARB establishes state air quality regulations which protect public health by addressing all major sources of smog-forming air pollution, and other forms of air pollution. As a result, cars today are 99 percent cleaner than in the 1970s, resulting in less air pollution overall, shorter hospital stays and fewer days missed from school and work due to respiratory and cardiopulmonary diseases.California regulations, based on extensive research and sound science, have driven innovation, leading to significant technological developments such as the catalytic converter (which helped slash ozone by 60 percent), and the production of highly marketable low- and zero-emission cars and trucks, and cleaner fuels.The Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006 (Nunez) expanded CARB’s role to development and oversight of California’s main greenhouse gas reduction programs. These include cap-and-trade, the Low Carbon Fuel Standard and the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) programs.

messages.text: Is the Secretary of State website compatible with older versions of web browsers?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The Secretary of State website works best when using Microsoft Internet Explorer (IE) 10.0 or higher or the latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, or Safari. If you are using an older version of any of these browsers, you may need to upgrade to the latest version. To upgrade your browser, go to browsehappy.com.

However, the text displays properly on the screen.

Weber, Ph.D.California Secretary of State Home  ความช่วยเหลือเกี่ยวกับเว็บไซด์  หน้าหลักของการขึ้นทะเบียนผู้ลงคะแนนเสียงทางออนไลน์ ความช่วยเหลือเกี่ยวกับเว็บไซด์ ความช่วยเหลือเกี่ยวกับเว็บไซด์ หน้านี้ให้ข้อมูลเกี่ยวกับข้อกำหนดในการดูเว็บไซด์การขึ้นทะเบียนผู้ลงคะแนนเสียงทางออนไลน์ของรัฐแคลิฟอร์เนีย (COVR) ข้อกำหนดด้านบราวเซอร์ การสนับสนุนการใช้งานบราวเซอร์ โปรแกรม COVR ทำงานได้ดีที่สุดเมื่อใช้ Microsoft Internet Explorer (IE) เวอร์ชั่น 8.0 หรือสูงกว่า หรือ Opera เวอร์ชั่น 10 หรือสูงกว่า หรือเวอร์ชั่นล่าสุดของ Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, หรือ Safari หากท่านกำลังใช้เวอร์ชั่นที่เก่ากว่าของบราวเซอร์ใดที่กล่าวมาแล้ว ท่านอาจจำเป็นต้องอัพเกรดเป็นเวอร์ชั่นล่าสุด หากต้องการอัพเกรดบราวเซอร์ของท่าน โปรดไปที่ https://browsehappy.com/ จาวาสคริปต์ (JavaScript) โปรแกรม COVR จำเป็นต้องใช้ JavaScript ที่เปิดใช้งานได้ในบราวเซอร์ของท่าน  หาก JavaScript ถูกระงับการใช้งาน ท่านจะไม่สามารถทำการขึ้นทะเบียนโดยใช้โปรแกรมออนไลน์ของเราได้ ท่านอาจ ดาวน์โหลดแบบฟอร์มการขึ้นทะเบียนที่สามารถพิมพ์ออกมาได้ เพื่อนำไปกรอกและส่งทางไปรษณีย์ โปรแกรมอ่านพีดีเอฟ (PDF Reader) โปรแกรม COVR มีลิงค์ไปยังเอกสารต่างๆ ที่อยู่ในรูปแบบพีดีเอฟ (PDF) ซึ่งไม่สามารถเปิดอ่านโดยเว็บบราวเซอร์ของท่านได้โดยตรง หากต้องการดาวน์โหลดและติดตั้งโปรแกรมอ่านพีดีเอฟฟรี ท่านสามารถไปที่เว็บไซด์: Acrobat Reader จาก Adobe - ทุกระบบปฏิบัติการ ดาวน์โหลดพีดีเอฟโดยใช้โปรแกรม Nitro PDF - ทุกระบบปฏิบัติการเพื่อดาวน์โหลดและติดตั้งโปรแกรมอ่านพีดีเอฟได้ฟรี เพื่อดาวน์โหลดและติดตั้งโปรแกรมอ่านพีดีเอฟได้ฟรี การใช้โปรแกรม COVR การใช้ตัวอ่านหน้าจอ หากท่านไม่สามารถไปยังหน้าถัดไป แสดงว่าท่านยังไม่ได้ตอบคำถามหนึ่งข้อที่กำหนดไว้ หากต้องการไปยังหน้าถัดไป ขอให้อ่านทบทวนใหม่ตั้งแต่ข้างบนเพื่อฟังคำแนะนำใดๆ หรือข้อความเตือนต่างๆ ที่จะช่วยในการตอบคำถามให้ครบถ้วน เมื่อตอบคำถามครบถ้วนแล้ว โปรแกรมจะเปิดให้ท่านไปยังหน้าต่อไปในการสัมภาษณ์ ตัวอักษรพิเศษ โปรแกรม COVR รองรับอักษรภาษาอังกฤษ (เช่น a, b, c, 1, 2, 3) และไม่รองรับอักษรพิเศษใดๆ ดังต่อไปนี้: ` ~ $ % ^ & * ( ) + = [ ] { } < > ? / \ | ปุ่มบราวเซอร์ "กลับไป (Back)" ใช้ปุ่ม "ก่อนหน้า (Previous)" และ "ถัดไป (Next)" ภายในโปรแกรมการขึ้นทะเบียน และอย่าใช้ปุ่มบราวเซอร์ "Back"สำนักงานเลขาธิการรัฐแคลิฟอร์เนียจะไม่รับผิดชอบต่อปัญหาด้านฮาร์ดแวร์หรือซอฟท์แวร์ใดอันเป็นผลมาจากการลงเครื่องมือใดๆ จากภายนอก ซึ่งรวมถึงเว็บบราวเซอร์ โปรแกรมเสริม (plug-ins) หรือการดาวน์โหลดที่ได้รับการแนะนำอื่นๆ แหล่งข้อมูลต่างๆ  ความช่วยเหลือเกี่ยวกับเว็บไซด์   ความเป็นส่วนตัว   การเข้าถึง  หน่วยงาน หน้าหลัก เกี่ยวกับ ธุรกิจ โนตารี่ และการตรวจสอบความถูกต้อง การเลือกตั้ง แคมเปญและการล็อบบี้ คลังข้อมูลของรัฐ สำนักทะเบียน ข่าว ติดต่อ แหล่งข้อมูล โอกาสทางอาชีพ ตารางบำรุงดูแลเว็บไซต์ แบบฟอร์มร้องทุกข์การเข้าถึงด้านภาษา คู่มือสำหรับการเข้าถึงบันทึกสาธารณะ โปรแกรมเปิดอ่านไฟล์ฟรี แผนผังเว็บไซต์ หน้าหลักรัฐแคลิฟอร์เนีย สายด่วนผู้ลงคะแนนเสียงเลือกตั้ง (855) 345-3933  Copyright © California Secretary of State  1500 11th Street, Sacramento, California 95814 (916) 653-6814 Back to Top ↑ Privacy Policy Website Help Accessibility

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: Can I choose cash payments over taking vacation time from work at the Secretary of State?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: No, vacation pay is at the same rate as an employee's regular salary or hourly pay, and all vacation pay is subject to tax withholding. Employees don't have the option of choosing cash payments over taking vacation time from work.

messages.text: What happens in the year of hire for vacation eligibility at the Secretary of State?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: In the year of hire, rehire, or conversion from supplemental to regular employment, vacation is based on the number of days worked during the year.

messages.text: How does the flexible work week schedule affect vacation earnings at the Secretary of State?

messages.speaker: agent

messages.text: What are the potential signs of life on the exoplanet Gliese 12 b?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Potential signs of life on an exoplanet, such as Gliese 12 b, could be detected through the mix of gases in the atmospheres of Earth-sized exoplanets. A strong indication of possible life would be the presence of gases like oxygen, carbon dioxide, and methane. Future telescopes might even pick up signs of photosynthesis or gases suggesting the presence of animal life. Intelligent, technological life might create atmospheric pollution, also detectable from afar.

contexts.text: Can We Find Life? - NASA Science But we’re looking.The big question – Is there life beyond Earth? – comes with an ironic asterisk: we don't really have a universally accepted definition of life itself. That said, we might not need one. We need only detect the telltale signs of life in an exoplanet atmosphere, and we have a better understanding of what those look like here on Earth.An artist's concept of what Kepler-1649c could look like from its surface.NASA/Ames Research Center/Daniel RutterWill we know life when we see it?The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, could get the first glimpses: the mix of gases in the atmospheres of Earth-sized exoplanets. Webb, or a similar spacecraft in the future, could pick up signs of an atmosphere like our own – oxygen, carbon dioxide, methane. A strong indication of possible life. Future telescopes might even pick up signs of photosynthesis – the transformation of light into chemical energy by plants – or even gases or molecules suggesting the presence of animal life. Intelligent, technological life might create atmospheric pollution, as it does on our planet, also detectable from afar. Of course, the best we might be able to manage is an estimate of probability. Still, an exoplanet with, say, a 95 percent probability of life would be a game changer of historic proportions.Artist's rendering of the James Webb Space Telescope.NASAHow will we find life?Life might turn up in our own neighborhood: beneath the Martian surface, perhaps, or in the dark, subsurface oceans of Jupiter's moon, Europa. Or maybe the dream of the ages will come true, and we'll eavesdrop on the communications of extraterrestrial civilizations. We might even capture evidence of "technosignatures," or traces of technology (think smog). Barring these strokes of luck, however, the job will be much harder. Light will be the key – light from the atmospheres of exoplanets, split up into a rainbow spectrum that we can read like a bar code.

NASA’s TESS Finds Intriguing World Sized Between Earth, Venus - NASA Science “Gliese 12 b represents one of the best targets to study whether Earth-size planets orbiting cool stars can retain their atmospheres, a crucial step to advance our understanding of habitability on planets across our galaxy,” said Shishir Dholakia, a doctoral student at the Centre for Astrophysics at the University of Southern Queensland in Australia. He co-led a different research team with Larissa Palethorpe, a doctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and University College London.Both teams suggest that studying Gliese 12 b may help unlock some aspects of our own solar system’s evolution.“It is thought that Earth’s and Venus’s first atmospheres were stripped away and then replenished by volcanic outgassing and bombardments from residual material in the solar system,” Palethorpe explained. “The Earth is habitable, but Venus is not due to its complete loss of water. Because Gliese 12 b is between Earth and Venus in temperature, its atmosphere could teach us a lot about the habitability pathways planets take as they develop.”One important factor in retaining an atmosphere is the storminess of its star. Red dwarfs tend to be magnetically active, resulting in frequent, powerful X-ray flares. However, analyses by both teams conclude that Gliese 12 shows no signs of extreme behavior.A paper led by Kuzuhara and Fukui was published May 23 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The Dholakia and Palethorpe findings were published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on the same day.During a transit, the host star’s light passes through any atmosphere. Different gas molecules absorb different colors, so the transit provides a set of chemical fingerprints that can be detected by telescopes like Webb. “We know of only a handful of temperate planets similar to Earth that are both close enough to us and meet other criteria needed for this kind of study, called transmission spectroscopy, using current facilities,” said Michael McElwain, a research astrophysicist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and a co-author of the Kuzuhara and Fukui paper. “To better understand the diversity of atmospheres and evolutionary outcomes for these planets, we need more examples like Gliese 12 b.”

NASA’s TESS Finds Intriguing World Sized Between Earth, Venus - NASA Science The newly discovered world, named Gliese 12 b, orbits every 12.8 days and is Earth’s size or slightly smaller — comparable to Venus. Assuming it has no atmosphere, the planet has a surface temperature estimated at around 107 degrees Fahrenheit (42 degrees Celsius).Astronomers say that the diminutive sizes and masses of red dwarf stars make them ideal for finding Earth-size planets. A smaller star means greater dimming for each transit, and a lower mass means an orbiting planet can produce a greater wobble, known as “reflex motion,” of the star. These effects make smaller planets easier to detect.Gliese 12 b’s estimated size may be as large as Earth or slightly smaller — comparable to Venus in our solar system. This artist’s concept compares Earth with different possible Gliese 12 b interpretations, from one with no atmosphere to one with a thick Venus-like one. Follow-up observations with NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope could help determine just how much atmosphere the planet retains as well as its composition.NASA/JPL-Caltech/R. Hurt (Caltech-IPAC)The lower luminosities of red dwarf stars also means their habitable zones — the range of orbital distances where liquid water could exist on a planet’s surface — lie closer to them. This makes it easier to detect transiting planets within habitable zones around red dwarfs than those around stars emitting more energy.The distance separating Gliese 12 and the new planet is just 7% of the distance between Earth and the Sun. The planet receives 1.6 times more energy from its star as Earth does from the Sun and about 85% of what Venus experiences.“Gliese 12 b represents one of the best targets to study whether Earth-size planets orbiting cool stars can retain their atmospheres, a crucial step to advance our understanding of habitability on planets across our galaxy,” said Shishir Dholakia, a doctoral student at the Centre for Astrophysics at the University of Southern Queensland in Australia. He co-led a different research team with Larissa Palethorpe, a doctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and University College London.Both teams suggest that studying Gliese 12 b may help unlock some aspects of our own solar system’s evolution.

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Gliese 12 b, being between Earth and Venus in temperature, could teach us a lot about the habitability pathways planets take as they develop. Its atmosphere could provide insights into the factors that make a planet habitable or not, such as the retention of an atmosphere and the presence or absence of water.

messages.text: What is the significance of the host star's storminess in the habitability of Gliese 12 b?

messages.speaker: agent

The planet receives 1.6 times more energy from its star as Earth does from the Sun and about 85% of what Venus experiences.“Gliese 12 b represents one of the best targets to study whether Earth-size planets orbiting cool stars can retain their atmospheres, a crucial step to advance our understanding of habitability on planets across our galaxy,” said Shishir Dholakia, a doctoral student at the Centre for Astrophysics at the University of Southern Queensland in Australia. He co-led a different research team with Larissa Palethorpe, a doctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and University College London.Both teams suggest that studying Gliese 12 b may help unlock some aspects of our own solar system’s evolution.

NASA’s TESS Finds Intriguing World Sized Between Earth, Venus - NASA Science Multiple factors make it a candidate well-suited for further study using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope.Gliese 12 b, which orbits a cool red dwarf star located just 40 light-years away, promises to tell astronomers more about how planets close to their stars retain or lose their atmospheres. In this artist’s concept, Gliese 12 b is shown retaining a thin atmosphere.NASA/JPL-Caltech/R. Hurt (Caltech-IPAC)TESS stares at a large swath of the sky for about a month at a time, tracking the brightness changes of tens of thousands of stars at intervals ranging from 20 seconds to 30 minutes. Capturing transits — brief, regular dimmings of stars caused by the passage of orbiting worlds — is one of the mission’s primary goals.“We’ve found the nearest, transiting, temperate, Earth-size world located to date,” said Masayuki Kuzuhara, a project assistant professor at the Astrobiology Center in Tokyo, who co-led one research team with Akihiko Fukui, a project assistant professor at the University of Tokyo. “Although we don’t yet know whether it possesses an atmosphere, we’ve been thinking of it as an exo-Venus, with similar size and energy received from its star as our planetary neighbor in the solar system.”The host star, called Gliese 12, is a cool red dwarf located almost 40 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The star is only about 27% of the Sun’s size, with about 60% of the Sun’s surface temperature. The newly discovered world, named Gliese 12 b, orbits every 12.8 days and is Earth’s size or slightly smaller — comparable to Venus. Assuming it has no atmosphere, the planet has a surface temperature estimated at around 107 degrees Fahrenheit (42 degrees Celsius).Astronomers say that the diminutive sizes and masses of red dwarf stars make them ideal for finding Earth-size planets. A smaller star means greater dimming for each transit, and a lower mass means an orbiting planet can produce a greater wobble, known as “reflex motion,” of the star.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What is RSS and how can it help me stay current?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: RSS, or Really Simple Syndication, is a technology that allows you to receive updates from websites in a standardized format. By using an RSS reader, you can stay current with news and updates from multiple websites in one place, without having to visit each site individually. The California Secretary of State's website provides a guide to getting started with RSS at http://infopeople.org/resources/rssinfo.html.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: What are the main types of wetlands that are the focus of protection in New York State?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The two main types of wetlands that are the focus of protection in New York State are tidal wetlands around Long Island, New York City and up the Hudson River all the way to Troy Dam; and freshwater wetlands found on river and lake floodplains across the state.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: And what kind of vegetation is adapted to these saturated soil conditions?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Wetlands are areas saturated by surface or ground water sufficient to support distinctive vegetation adapted for life in saturated soil conditions. The specific types of vegetation can vary, but they are all plants that are able to thrive in wet and often muddy conditions.

messages.text: How does the DEC regulate wetlands in New York State?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) regulates wetlands through the state Freshwater Wetlands Act. This act includes provisions for wetlands mapping and sets forth guidelines for the protection and conservation of wetlands. The DEC also has the authority to issue permits for activities that may impact wetlands, such as construction projects.

messages.text: Can I go fishing in these wetland areas?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Yes, fishing is allowed in wetland areas in New York State, as long as you follow the state's fishing regulations. Freshwater fishing and saltwater fishing are both popular activities in New York, and there are many different species of fish that can be found in wetland areas. However, it's important to note that some wetland areas may have specific restrictions on fishing to protect sensitive species or habitats.

messages.speaker: user
messages.text: How does New York State categorize its waterbodies?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: New York State categorizes its waterbodies into four main groups: watersheds, lakes and rivers, oceans and estuaries, and wetlands. Each of these categories includes a wide variety of different waterbodies, from small streams and ponds to large lakes and extensive ocean coastlines. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) provides information and resources for each of these categories on its website.

contexts.text: Waterbodies - NYSDEC Wetlands serve as natural habitat for many species of plants and animals and absorb the forces of flood and tidal erosion to prevent loss of upland soil.In New York State, two main types of wetlands are the focus of protection: tidal wetlands around Long Island, New York City and up the Hudson River all the way to Troy Dam; and freshwater wetlands found on river and lake floodplains across the state.This website provides information about:The status of New York's tidal and freshwater wetlands, and trends in the extent of wetlands in the stateThe state Freshwater Wetlands Act and how DEC regulates wetlands, including wetlands mappingWetlands conservation and restoration Explore Waterbodies in New York State New York State has countless waterbodies including watersheds, lakes and rivers, oceans and estuaries, and wetlands. Waterbodies - NYSDEC What you do at your house affects everyone downstream and around you.Find watersheds facts and reports about NYS watersheds.Lakes and RiversNew York State is richly endowed with freshwater lakes, ponds and reservoirs, as well as portions of two of the five Great Lakes and thousands of miles of rivers and streams.These inland water bodies serve as the drinking water supplies, provide flood control to protect life and property, and support recreation, tourism, agriculture, fishing, power generation, and manufacturing. These water bodies also provide habitat for aquatic plant and animal life.Oceans and EstuariesNew York has shoreline on the Northern Atlantic Ocean that connects to tidal and freshwater rivers and streams that drain through watersheds into the ocean. Within the Hudson Valley, New York City, and Long Island there are several distinct estuaries that serve as valuable habitat for marine life while providing essential human services to coastal communities and the regional economy.There are five major estuaries in New York State:Peconic Bays systemLong Island south shore bays systemNew York/New Jersey HarborHudson River EstuaryLong Island SoundDEC, along with EPA, other state agencies, and local municipalities devised management plans for each of these areas to address their issues of concern and develop protection and restoration strategies.WetlandsWetlands (swamps, marshes, bogs, and similar areas) are areas saturated by surface or ground water sufficient to support distinctive vegetation adapted for life in saturated soil conditions. messages.text: That sounds fascinating! Can students build real rovers to explore other planets in the future?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: While AI language models like me can't predict the future, I can tell you that there are ongoing efforts to involve students in space exploration. For instance, NASA's "Mission to Mars Student Challenge" allows students to plan, design, and build their own missions to the Red Planet and tag along for the ride as a rover lands on Mars. Additionally, designing and building landers, rovers, and spacecraft is a significant part of many aerospace engineering programs in universities worldwide.

Student Project: Code a Mars Sample Collection Video Game | NASA/JPL Edu Rovers on Mars aren’t controlled with joysticks or keyboards. But in the future, astronauts in orbit around Mars or on the surface of the planet could use remote controls to drive rovers. Your game can use keys on the keyboard to make the rover drive. Tasks Make the rover move up, down, left, and right on the screen using four different keys on the keyboard. Hint: See if a block in the Events section will help. (See example image.) Specify how far the rover will move each time one of those keys is pressed. Select a distance that makes the rover movement appear smooth when the key is pressed and held. Hint: See if a block in the Motion section will help. (See example image.) Make the rover rotate so it points in the direction of travel. Bonus: Make the rover move diagonally using keys other than the keys already assigned. + Expand image 3. Add sample tubes for collection Sample tubes contain valuable rock samples collected by the Perseverance Mars rover and left behind for a fetch rover to collect. You should add sample collection tubes to your game to provide destinations for your rover. By studying the backdrop images closely, you can identify areas that look interesting and place sample tubes in those spots. Tasks Add three or more sample tube sprites to visit during gameplay by placing the downloaded sample tube sprites to the backdrop by selecting Upload sprite the same way you did in Step 1. Make the sample tube sprites disappear when they are visited by the rover. Hint: See if a block in the Control section will help. (See example image.) Make the sample tube sprites reappear when players click the green flag to restart the game. + Expand image 4. Add a countdown timer NASA’s missions to Mars and other destinations have a planned life expectancy. Some missions, including every Mars rover to date, have been extended and operated beyond their planned mission life expectancy, while others experience problems that shorten their mission. You can create a timer that counts down to the end of the mission and ends the game.

messages.text: What are some of the interesting areas on Mars where I can collect samples in the Mars Sample Collection Video Game?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The Mars Sample Collection Video Game offers various interesting areas for sample collection. To identify these spots, I would recommend studying the backdrop images closely. You can place sample tubes in areas that look intriguing, such as spots with unique rock formations or different terrain types. These sample collection tubes serve as destinations for your rover to visit during gameplay.

Student Project: Code a Mars Sample Collection Video Game | NASA/JPL Edu Rovers on Mars aren’t controlled with joysticks or keyboards. But in the future, astronauts in orbit around Mars or on the surface of the planet could use remote controls to drive rovers. Your game can use keys on the keyboard to make the rover drive. Tasks Make the rover move up, down, left, and right on the screen using four different keys on the keyboard. Hint: See if a block in the Events section will help. (See example image.) Specify how far the rover will move each time one of those keys is pressed. Select a distance that makes the rover movement appear smooth when the key is pressed and held. Hint: See if a block in the Motion section will help. (See example image.) Make the rover rotate so it points in the direction of travel. Bonus: Make the rover move diagonally using keys other than the keys already assigned. + Expand image 3. Add sample tubes for collection Sample tubes contain valuable rock samples collected by the Perseverance Mars rover and left behind for a fetch rover to collect. You should add sample collection tubes to your game to provide destinations for your rover. By studying the backdrop images closely, you can identify areas that look interesting and place sample tubes in those spots. Tasks Add three or more sample tube sprites to visit during gameplay by placing the downloaded sample tube sprites to the backdrop by selecting Upload sprite the same way you did in Step 1. Make the sample tube sprites disappear when they are visited by the rover. Hint: See if a block in the Control section will help. (See example image.) Make the sample tube sprites reappear when players click the green flag to restart the game. + Expand image 4. Add a countdown timer NASA’s missions to Mars and other destinations have a planned life expectancy. Some missions, including every Mars rover to date, have been extended and operated beyond their planned mission life expectancy, while others experience problems that shorten their mission. You can create a timer that counts down to the end of the mission and ends the game.

Student Project: Code a Mars Sample Collection Video Game | NASA/JPL Edu Materials Computer with internet accessFree Scratch accountMars fetch rover sprite – Download PNGMars sample collection tube sprite – Download PNG Jezero crater surface images – Download ZIP 1. Get set up Download the Jezero Crater surface images, the Mars sample collection tube image, and Mars fetch rover sprite image, and save them to a computer. Unzip the surface images zip file into a new folder. On the Scratch website, click Create to begin a new project. (Sign in or create an account if you want to save your work so you can revisit or redesign your game in the future.) Create a new backdrop by moving the mouse over Choose a Backdrop in the Stage window and selecting Upload Backdrop. Pick the Jezero Crater surface image of your choice. The Stage area of the screen should now display your selected backdrop image. (See example image.) Create a new sprite by moving the mouse over Choose a sprite in the Sprite window and selecting Upload sprite. Choose the Mars fetch rover sprite image. There should now be a rover placed over your backdrop image along with the original cat sprite. (See example image.) Delete the existing cat sprite by clicking on it in the Sprites window and clicking the “x” in the corner. With the rover sprite selected, you’re ready to create the code that manages the game and controls the rover!+ Expand image 2. Make the rover drive NASA explores Mars with orbiters that travel around the planet, stationary landers on the ground, and rovers that can travel many miles on the surface. For rovers to visit more than one place on Mars, they must be able to drive. Rovers on Mars aren’t controlled with joysticks or keyboards. But in the future, astronauts in orbit around Mars or on the surface of the planet could use remote controls to drive rovers. Your game can use keys on the keyboard to make the rover drive. Tasks Make the rover move up, down, left, and right on the screen using four different keys on the keyboard. Hint: See if a block in the Events section will help.

messages.text: What do I do with the sample tubes once I collect samples in the Mars Sample Collection Video Game?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Once you collect samples using the sample tubes in the Mars Sample Collection Video Game, the tubes should disappear when visited by the rover. To continue collecting samples, you can make the sample tube sprites reappear when players click the green flag to restart the game. This way, you can keep exploring and collecting samples throughout your Martian adventure.

messages.text: I'd love to learn more about the geology of Mars. Are there any activities that help me explore Mars' geology like a NASA scientist?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Yes, there are activities that allow you to explore Mars' geology similar to a NASA scientist. For instance, you can create a sedimentary "rock" from play dough and investigate it using your geology skills with the "Explore Rocks Using Core Sampling" project at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory website. This project helps you understand the processes that create rocks and how scientists study them, both on Earth and on Mars.

Student Project: Code a Mars Sample Collection Video Game | NASA/JPL Edu Rovers on Mars aren’t controlled with joysticks or keyboards. But in the future, astronauts in orbit around Mars or on the surface of the planet could use remote controls to drive rovers. Your game can use keys on the keyboard to make the rover drive. Tasks Make the rover move up, down, left, and right on the screen using four different keys on the keyboard. Hint: See if a block in the Events section will help. (See example image.) Specify how far the rover will move each time one of those keys is pressed. Select a distance that makes the rover movement appear smooth when the key is pressed and held. Hint: See if a block in the Motion section will help. (See example image.) Make the rover rotate so it points in the direction of travel. Bonus: Make the rover move diagonally using keys other than the keys already assigned. + Expand image 3. Add sample tubes for collection Sample tubes contain valuable rock samples collected by the Perseverance Mars rover and left behind for a fetch rover to collect. You should add sample collection tubes to your game to provide destinations for your rover. By studying the backdrop images closely, you can identify areas that look interesting and place sample tubes in those spots. Tasks Add three or more sample tube sprites to visit during gameplay by placing the downloaded sample tube sprites to the backdrop by selecting Upload sprite the same way you did in Step 1. Make the sample tube sprites disappear when they are visited by the rover. Hint: See if a block in the Control section will help. (See example image.) Make the sample tube sprites reappear when players click the green flag to restart the game. + Expand image 4. Add a countdown timer NASA’s missions to Mars and other destinations have a planned life expectancy. Some missions, including every Mars rover to date, have been extended and operated beyond their planned mission life expectancy, while others experience problems that shorten their mission. You can create a timer that counts down to the end of the mission and ends the game.

messages.text: How do rovers like Perseverance communicate with Earth and send the data they collect?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Rovers like Perseverance communicate with Earth using NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN), which consists of large, high-precision radio antennas located in California, Spain, and Australia. These antennas communicate with spacecraft using radio signals, enabling data transfer between the rovers and Earth. It's fascinating to think about the technology and infrastructure that allow us to explore other planets.

messages.text: What are the data collections returned for the Hayabusa mission and what are the instruments used in the mission?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: The Hayabusa mission returned data collections from the Asteroid Multi-band Imaging Camera (AMICA), the Near Infrared Spectrometer (NIRS), and the Light Detection and Ranging Instrument (LIDAR). The instruments used in the mission include the High Resolution Instrument (HRI), the Medium Resolution Instrument (MRI), the Asteroid Multi-band Imaging Camera (AMICA), the Near Infrared Spectrometer (NIRS), and the Light Detection and Ranging Instrument (LIDAR).

NASA - NSSDCA - Spacecraft - Details The insulated and cushioned re-entry capsule, 40 cm in diameter and 25 cm deep with a mass of about 20 kg, is attached to the body of the spacecraft near the sample collection horn. The capsule has a convex nose covered with a 3 cm thick ablative heat shield to protect the samples from the high velocity (~13 km/s) re-entry. Cost of the Hayabusa spacecraft is roughly 12 billion yen ($100 million U.S.) Surface Sample Collection The lander will be equipped with a universal sample collection device which will gather roughly one gram of surface samples taken from the landings at 3 different locations. The device consists of a funnel-shaped collection horn, 40 cm in diameter at the end, which is to be placed over the sampling area. A pyrotechnic device fires a 10 gram metal projectile down the barrel of the horn at 200 - 300 m/sec. The projectile strikes the surface producing a small impact crater in the surface of the asteroid and propelling ejecta fragments back up the horn, where some of it is funnelled into a sample collection chamber. Prior to each sampling run, the spacecraft will drop a small target plate onto the surface from about 30 m altitude to use as a landmark to ensure the relative horizontal velocity between the spacecraft and asteroid surface is zero during the sampling. After sampling the samples will be stored in the re-entry capsule for return to Earth. Minerva The Minerva lander is a small (591 gram) cylinder about the size of a coffee can, designed to be released from the spacecraft on the first rehearsal touchdown run. It has the ability to "hop" on the surface of the asteroid and has full autonomy. It is equipped with an imaging system comprising three miniature cameras and temperature measuring devices. Data will be relayed to Hayabusa and then to Earth. SSV Rover The rover, or Small Science Vehicle (SSV), was to have been a NASA contribution to the mission but was cancelled due to budget contraints. The SSV would have been dropped onto the surface of the asteroid by the Hayabusa spacecraft.

Data will be relayed to Hayabusa and then to Earth. NASA - NSSDCA - Experiment - Details NASA - NSSDCA - Experiment - Details Saturday, 25 May 2024 Asteroid Multi-band Imaging Camera (AMICA)NSSDCA ID: 2003-019A-01Mission Name: HayabusaPrincipal Investigator:Dr. Tsuko NakamuraDescriptionThe Asteroid Multi-band Imaging Camera (AMICA) on Hayabusa is designed to collect scientific images and also to be used for optical navigation. The AMICA system consists of a refracting telescope, a filter wheel, a CCD, and associated electronics. The total assembly is mounted on the corner of the bottom-facing deck of the spacecraft near the sampler horn and measures 12.0 x 13.5 x 18.0 cm. AMICA has a field-of-view of 5.7 x 5.7 degrees giving a frame size of about 1 km at 10 km range. The camera assembly has a mass of 1.74 kg. The optical system is a refracting telescope with five lenses behind a quartz optical parallel window. The focal length is 120 mm and the effective lens diameter is 15 mm (F/8.0). Mounted at the end of the telescope is a filter wheel with eight positions. Each filter is sector-shaped and can be rotated into position behind the telescope. Seven of the filters cover the ECAS system bands: ul, b, v, w, x, p, and zs. There is also a closeup lens (also v-filter) to be used during the sampling phase. After passing through the filter, the image falls on a frame-transfer CCD. The CCD is a back-illuminated multi-pinned phase type, 1024 x 1000 pixels. A single pixel sees 20 arcsec. 30 different exposure times ranging from 5.5 ms to 134 s are available, and there is a ~1 microsecond exposure time to correct readout smear. Four position-angle glass polarizers are mounted on one edge of the CCD chip covering 200 x 200 pixels each. These allow measurement of polarization of the asteroid in the v- and w-bands. The associated electronics include a computer for data compression and image data processing.

messages.text: What are the goals of collaborative courts in Tuolumne County and what are some examples of these courts?

messages.speaker: agent
messages.text: Collaborative courts in Tuolumne County aim to promote accountability through judicial supervision and monitoring. They are trauma-focused, culturally sensitive, and emphasize early intervention, ongoing supervision, and frequent judicial reviews. The goals are to address substance abuse and mental health issues, connect participants to available community services, seek alternatives to incarceration and other forms of punishment, and reduce recidivism.  Some examples of these courts include CARE Court, Adult Drug Court, and Dependency Drug Court. CARE Court connects a person struggling with untreated mental illness and often also substance use challenges with a court-ordered Care Plan for up to 24 months. Adult Drug Court is a collaboration of agencies that provides an alternative to incarceration for defendants who meet the program's eligibility criteria. Dependency Drug Court is a collaborative program between the Tuolumne Superior Court Juvenile Division, Behavioral Health Services, and CWS, designed to support the parent in addressing their Substance Use Disorder needs.

This includes collaborative or “problem-solving” courts, also known as therapeutic justice courts. This type of court is intended to promote accountability through judicial supervision and monitoring. These collaborative courts (also called problem-solving courts, therapeutic justice courts, judicially led diversion programs, and recovery-oriented compliance dockets) are characterized by a team approach which brings together resources from the court’s justice partners and community organizations. Collaborative courts are trauma-focused, culturally sensitive, and emphasize early intervention, ongoing supervision, and frequent judicial reviews. The goals are to address substance abuse and mental health issues, connect participants to available community services, seek alternatives to incarceration and other forms of punishment, and reduce recidivism. National and state studies have shown that collaborative courts generate substantial savings within the justice system by increasing case processing efficiencies and reducing incarceration costs. Tuolumne County Superior Court is committed to continuing to develop and refine these programs as part of its overall strategy to increase access to justice. CARE Court  CARE Court connects a person struggling with untreated mental illness – and often also substance use challenges – with a court-ordered Care Plan for up to 24 months. Using the Drug Court Model, DDC provides close monitoring by the Court and Dependency Drug Court Treatment Team, frequent substance abuse testing, and extensive support and structure. Parent’s needs are assessed individually with a treatment plan designed to meet those needs and support the goal of Family Reunification/Family Maintenance. Dependency Drug Court runs concurrent with the full term of the time spent in Family Reunification Services, and during Family Maintenance. DDC operates as a collaborative program, which includes Child Welfare Services case workers, clinical staff, a Court coordinator, and the Juvenile Court Judge. The treatment team communicates regularly regarding the progress and participation of DDC participants. The Treatment Team assembles monthly, prior to the court session, at which time the group reviews each case and makes decisions concerning visits, treatment, program compliance and progress towards graduation. Dependency Drug Court clients appear in front of the Juvenile Court Judge monthly. In the first weeks of the program, participants may be required to attend one or more hearings concerning the legal aspects of dependency proceedings. If there are issues related to compliance arising during treatment, participants may be required to appear in court more often.  Was this helpful?  Yes No
